passages.original: ,Hoc idem in indefinilis propositionibusexspectandumest.Nam dividuntinter severum falsumque, ut si quis dicat homo bipes est, vera est, homo bipes non est, falsa est, et item homo quadrupes est, falsa est, homo quadrupes non est, vera est; verae autem simul inveniri possunt, ut si quis dicat homo grammaticus est, si quis hoc dicat de Donato, verum est. Item homo grammaticus non est, si quis hoc dicat de Catone, verum est, ut simul falsæ sint nunquam reperie.Dus HiOl',quoque ostenditur indefinitas cum particularibus aequali esse potentia. Amplius quod dictum est, contrajacentes, id est universalem affirmativam et particularem negativam, et item universalem negativam et particularem affirmativam neque veras simul esse neque falsas, sed inter se divi- dere verum falsumque, hoc idem evenit in indefinitis.
passages.english: The same is to be expected in indefinite propositions. For they divide true and false between them: if someone says "man is two-footed," it is true; "man is not two-footed," it is false; and likewise "man is four-footed" is false, "man is not four-footed" is true. But they can be found true together: if someone says "man is a grammarian," and says this of Donatus, it is true. Likewise "man is not a grammarian," if someone says this of Cato, it is true; but you will never find them false together. By this too it is shown that indefinites are of equal force with particulars. Further, what was said about contradictories (contraiacentes), that is, the universal affirmative and the particular negative, and likewise the universal negative and the particular affirmative, that they are neither true together nor false together, but divide true and false between them, this same thing happens in the indefinites.
passages.notes: "reperie.Dus HiOl',quoque" is garbled; read as "reperies. Hinc quoque" ("you will find. Hence too"). "Contrajacentes" is Boethius' term for contradictory opposites.

passages.original: Conversis igitur primis posterisque extremitatibus primae figuræ,tertiavelsecunda figura nascuntur.At vero unaquæque horum trium figurarum habet sub se plures syllogismorum modos, ut modi sub figuris ita sint ut sunt species sub suis generibus. Habet enim prima figura sub se,Aristotele auctore, modos quatuor ; sed Theophrastus vel Eudemus super hos quatuor quinque alios mo- i dos addunt,Aristotele dante principium in secundo priorum Analyticorum volumine,quod melius postmodum explicabilur.Secunda vero figura habet sub se quatuor modos ; tertia vero, auctore Aristotele, sex ; addunt etiam alii unum,sicut ipse Porphyrius, superiores scilicet sequens. Et quoniam (ut superiore libro dictum est) aliae propositionesaffirmativae sunt, aliae negativae, et earum aliæ universales, aliae vero particulares,secundum eas ipsas,propositiones syllogismorumconclusionesquejunguntur.Namque primae figurae primus modus est qui fit ex duabus universalibus alfirmativis,universalem colligens affirmativam.Si enim a terminus fuerit in omni b termino,et si b terminus de omni c termino fuerit prae- dicatus,aterminus de omni ctermino praedicabitur.
passages.english: So when the first and last extremes of the first figure are converted, the third or the second figure arises. But each of these three figures has under it several moods of syllogisms, so that the moods stand under the figures as species stand under their genera. For the first figure has under it, on Aristotle's authority, four moods; but Theophrastus or Eudemus add five other moods to these four, Aristotle having provided the starting point in the second volume of the Prior Analytics, which will be better explained later. The second figure has under it four moods, and the third, on Aristotle's authority, six; others also add one, as Porphyry himself does, following, that is, his predecessors. And since (as was said in the previous book) some propositions are affirmative, others negative, and of these some are universal, others particular, the propositions and conclusions of syllogisms are combined according to these very [kinds]. For the first mood of the first figure is the one made from two universal affirmatives, concluding a universal affirmative. For if term a is in every term b, and if term b is predicated of every term c, term a will be predicated of every term c.

passages.original: Illud vero quod dictum est, per ipsa quae posita sunt, hoc propter eos dictum est qui tales faciunt syllogismos, in quibus aut minus aliquid, aut plus, aut aliud propositum est quam proponi debuerat. Fiunt enim hujusmodi syllogismi. Si quis enim ita dicat: Socrates homo est, omnis homo animal est, et concludat, Socrates igitur animatus est, minus proposuit, quod non dixit omne animal esse animatum. Nunc si sic proposuisset, recte Socrates animatum esse concluderet, ita dicendo : Socrates homo est, omnis homo animal est, et omne animal animatum est, Socrates igitur animatus est.
passages.english: As for the phrase "through the very things that have been posited," this was said on account of those who construct syllogisms in which either something less, or more, or something other has been put forward than ought to have been put forward. For syllogisms of this kind do occur. For if someone were to say: "Socrates is a man, every man is an animal," and were to conclude, "therefore Socrates is animate," he has put forward too little, since he did not say that every animal is animate. Now if he had put it forward thus, he would rightly conclude that Socrates is animate, saying as follows: "Socrates is a man, every man is an animal, and every animal is animate; therefore Socrates is animate."
passages.notes: "Through the very things that have been posited" (per ipsa quae posita sunt) quotes a phrase from the definition of the syllogism under discussion.

passages.original: Vel certe sic, quia superius talem syllogismum diximus terminis com mutatis, quem Aristoteles dissimi lem non putat.
passages.english: Or certainly thus, because above we stated such a syllogism with the terms interchanged, which Aristotle does not consider different.
